quickId: Glossy evergreen leaves, finely toothed, smaller and narrower than japonica camellia
Blooms in fall (Oct–Dec), unlike japonicas that bloom mid-winter to spring
Ruffled white double flowers with yellow center; round green buds
lookalikes: Japonica camellia: larger, broader leaves; blooms later in winter and spring.
facts: Sasanquas are the fall-blooming camellias.
'Mine-no-yuki' is a common white double sasanqua in Lowcountry yards.
care: Prune right after blooming in late winter; later pruning removes next fall's buds. Check leaf undersides for tea scale (white fuzzy coating).

quickId: Multi-trunk vase shape with smooth, peeling, cinnamon-colored bark
Small oval leaves that turn orange and red in fall
Summer clusters of crinkled flowers; round seed capsules into winter
lookalikes: Its smooth, muscular multi-trunks are very distinctive. Few lookalikes in the yard.
facts: Blooms on new growth, so late-winter pruning doesn't cost flowers.
Topping all trunks at one height ("crepe murder") causes knuckles and weak sprouts.
care: Prune mid-Feb to early March. Remove suckers, dead and crossing branches, thin the interior, limb up the trunks. Take no more than about 1/4 of the canopy per year.

quickId: Low, clumping fan palm with no tall trunk; trunks creep along the ground
Silvery blue-green fan-shaped leaves
Leaf stems lined with small sharp teeth (the "saw")
lookalikes: Blue Mediterranean fan palm: stiffer, more deeply split leaves and short upright trunks. Dwarf palmetto (Sabal minor): smooth stems, greener.
facts: Native to the Southeast coast and tolerant of drought, heat, salt, and sandy soil.
The silver form is prized in Lowcountry landscaping.
care: Once a year, cut dead brown fronds at the base. Wear gloves. Never remove green fronds.

quickId: Rosette of stiff, narrow, dark-green sword-like leaves on a short trunk
Needle-sharp leaf tips
Fine saw-toothed leaf edges that feel rough
lookalikes: Spanish dagger / mound lily (Yucca gloriosa): wider, bluer, flexible leaves with smooth edges and softer tips. Often blooms in fall.
facts: Native along the Southeast coast.
Tall spikes of creamy white flowers in late spring or early summer.
Trunks can reach 8–10 ft. Cut pieces root easily.
care: Mind the tips near walkways; clipping the points is fine. Remove dead lower leaves with loppers, long sleeves, and eye protection.

quickId: Glossy, leathery oval leaves in opposite pairs
Leaves often a bit wavy or cupped, with a pale midrib
Blue-black berries in fall and winter
lookalikes: Yaupon holly has much smaller leaves; sweet olive often has toothed leaves.
facts: One of the most common foundation and hedge shrubs in coastal SC.
Considered invasive in SC: birds spread its berries.
Strong-scented white flower clusters in late spring.
care: Light shaping anytime in the growing season, narrower at top than bottom. Hard rejuvenation in late winter. It tolerates a cut to 12–18 in. Pull seedlings.

quickId: Grows on salt marsh edges
Gray-green leaves; upper leaves narrow
Females turn silvery-white with fluffy seed tufts in fall
lookalikes: False willow (Baccharis angustifolia): narrower, willow-like leaves, same marshes and same fall show.
facts: Male and female plants are separate. Only females get fluffy.
Late flowers feed migrating monarchs.
Very salt-tolerant and helps stabilize marsh edges. Mildly toxic to livestock.
care: A wild native. Leave it be.

quickId: Tall, dense stands of broad, flat grass blades
Leaf edges are saw-toothed and will cut skin
Freshwater tidal marsh, often in old rice fields
lookalikes: Wild rice (Zizania aquatica): soft leaf edges and big airy seed heads in late summer. Cultivated rice doesn't persist in the wild here.
facts: Spreads by thick rhizomes into nearly pure stands.
A main plant that took over Waccamaw rice fields after cultivation ended.
Gives cover to marsh birds and wildlife.
care: Wear long sleeves walking through it.

quickId: Flared, buttressed trunk base, often standing in water
Cypress "knees" poking up around it
Soft needles that turn rusty-brown and drop in fall (a deciduous conifer)
lookalikes: Pond cypress (Taxodium ascendens): needles pressed close to twigs, more often in still ponds.
facts: Some Black River cypress are over 2,000 years old.
Big stumps on the Waccamaw are mostly from logging in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
The Spanish moss hanging on it is a bromeliad, not a moss, and doesn't harm the tree.
care: A wild native. Enjoy it from the water.
